file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/78report.htm[29-08-2018 16:15:19]
 species and also reduces the availability of fodder to the wild animals and to the livestock.
30. The Committee recommends that in order to augment the household income in rural areas and reduce their
 dependence on forests the Ministry should take effective measures towards development of non-timber forests
 resources and also fund projects for carrying out afforestation programme on private lands.
31. The Committee does not fully share the findings of the Survey of India for nature has its own regulatory
 system. Seen in proper perspective, the fuel wood collection by villagers or tribals living near the forests is an
 activity which has been going on ever since the man set its foot on the earth. This activity by tribals or villagers,
 the Committee feels, only helps in the regeneration of the land thus adding indirectly to the growth of the forests.
 Likewise the dry leaves also contribute to the process for they ultimately convert into a kind of manure that is
 conducive to the growth of forests. The Committee does not agree to the view the animal footing and grazing
 affects the tender plants. On the other hand there is a remote possibility of such tender plants being there in a
 dense forest unless they are planted as a part of the planned forestry. In fact, a forest is nothing but a wild
 growth which has sprung up as a part of normal process of the nature. Again, seen in a proper perspective, the
 grazing by animals is indirectly an activity equal to the filling of land which should help the reproductive
 process.
32. The Committee observes that as a result of persistent recommendation of the Committee or otherwise on
 merits the rights of tribals and villagers etc. living near the forests to collect the fuel wood have at least being
 recognized by no less a person than the Prime Minister of the country. The Ministry should therefore fall in line
 and recognize these rights which only help, as stated above, in the growth of forests as part of a natural activity.
33. Animal grazing is also not an activity which would affect the growth of the forests. Apart from what has been
 said above, the animal excreta ultimately converts itself into a kind of manure which would help the growth of
 forests.
34. The Committee further observes that the Ministry should in fact concentrate on organized felling of trees
 undertaken on a large scale by timber smugglers in connivance with the forest authorities. If checked properly,
 this alone would go a long way in saving the forests.
WILDLIFE (PROTECTION) ACT,1972
35. The Committee was informed that the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 in its present form is quite effective,
 particularly, in dealing with persons violating the provision of the Act. According to Section 51 of the Act, punishment
 for violating any of the provisions of the Act may extend to 3 years of imprisonment or with a fine which may extend
 up to Rs.25,000/- or both. In case an offence is committed in relation to any animal specified in Schedule I or Part II of
 Schedule II of the Act or whether the offence relates to hunting in or altering the boundaries of a Sanctuary or a
 National Park, such offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than one year and also with a fine not
 less than Rs.5,000/-. The term of imprisonment can extend up to six years In case of a second or subsequent offence,
 the term of imprisonment can extend to 6 years and shall not be less than 2 years and the amount of fine shall not be
 less than Rs.10,000/-. The term of imprisonment for persons indulging in illegal trade or species included in Schedule I
 or Part n of Schedule II can extend up to 7 years and also with a fine which shall not be less than Rs.5,000/-. In addition
 to the above deterrent measures, there is a provision to forfeit to the State Government any trap, tool vehicle, vessel or
 weapon used in committing the offence.
36. The Committee is of the view that the above mentioned provisions should constantly be kept in view taking
 into account the experiences gained in operation of these provisions. While the Wildlife needs to be protected
 from the onslaughts of the man, a balance has also to be maintained in the penal provisions of the law. The penal
 provisions if they are made more stringent will only encourage corruption. There is a need to discourage the
 tendency of amending the Act on the basis of individual incidents. On the other hand the experience gained over
 a period of time should form the basis of a review of various provisions.

Positive impact of floods:

 refineries were directed to comply with the specifications.

79th Report on the Information Technology Bill, 1999
 
 The Chairman, Rajya Sabha in pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
 Committees, referred* the Information Technology Bill, 1999**, as introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16 th December,
 1999 and pending therein, to the Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests for
 examination and Report.
2. In the present day world it has been the electronics and now the Information Technology (IT) which influence our life
 the most. There is hardly any area of human endeavour where electronic gadgets have not reached. There is barely any
 industry which does not depend, for its efficiency and productivity, on the application of electronics in its different
 manifestations. Technology has emerged as the vehicle of rapid change in the work culture and the way mankind
 communicates in the century. India has been no exception to this phenomenon. Whether in the field of
 telecommunications, roads, ports or air travel, the hallmark has been more efficient and cost effective technology. Thus
 from slow-moving majestic automobiles the country has moved to smart and fast technologies which have given us
 much more advanced vehicles, coal guzzling steam locomotives which have been replaced by electric traction engines.
3. Information Technology is a product of information age and technology. It is a vehicle for future development,
 opportunities, challenges and competition that enables faster collection and dissemination of information. In the history
 of civilization, no work of science has had so comprehensive an impact on human development as IT. Undoubtedly, IT
 has been the greatest changing agent of this century and promises to play its role even more dramatically in the times to
 come. IT is changing every aspect of human life, breaking old barriers and building new inter connections in the
 emerging global village and becoming the chief determinant of progress of nations and that of individuals. IT is being
 meaningfully employed in railways and airlines, banking, insurance, weather forecasting, radio astronomy, molecular
 biology, aerodynamics, etc. thereby reducing the fatigue and increasing the productivity and efficiency. And in
 education too, IT has a vital role. A large variety of software is available to cater to self-learning and evaluation on
 various subjects.
4. IT is a broad term covering the entire gamut of managing and processing information. Computer hardware, software
 and internet are the tools for the systems that have been designed, developed, supported or managed by IT
 professionals. The discovery of computers and subsequent development of the technology popularly known as
 information technology is one of the most significant achievements of the 20
th century. The role of IT as an instrument
 for progress and development has been acknowledged widely and is expected to bring in major social and economic
 benefits for the mankind and accelerate the process of development.
 
 
 
* Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II, dated the 14
th January, 2000
** Annexure
 
 
 
 

79th Report on the Information Technology Bill, 1999
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/79report.htm[29-08-2018 16:16:19]
5. Andhra Pradesh is an example of how the States in the country can incorporate IT in the day-to-day functioning of the
 Government and re-engineer the manner in which services are provided to citizens. Under its ‘One-stop non-stop’
 approach, a pilot project called Twin cities Integrated Network Service (TWINS) integrated 18 services of six
 departments over one counter. It provides fast and easy access to Government services, makes the access to
 Government much simpler and can also cut down on corruption. It would be naive, of course, to suggest IT as the
 ultimate panacea for corruption, which may find ingenious ways to beat new technology.
6. Today, among the major Asian industrialized countries, India has abundant technically skilled manpower towards
 global IT development. IT is the fastest emerging industrial segment in the country. During the last decade, IT sector
 has registered an unprecedented growth. All the renowned global brands have either established production facilities in
 the country or are present in the market through technical/financial collaborations, thus giving consumer a wider choice
 of products in terms of features, quality and prices.
7. A special Task Force on Information Technology and Software Development involving several agencies at Central
 and State levels has been constituted with a view to keep pace with the latest technology developments abroad. To that
 end Government have taken two major initiatives, one, the formation of IT Ministry at the Central level and second the
 establishment of a Rs.100 crores National Venture Fund for software and IT industry. The IT industry is thus expected
 to play a lead role and serve as a nodal point to facilitate further development of IT industry.
8. Member countries of the United Nations have recognised the need for "Uniformity of laws applicable to alternatives
 to paper-based methods of communications and storage of information". A model law on e-commerce was adopted in
 1996 by the U.N. Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITAL) and the U.N. General Assembly recommended
 to its members in 1997 to give due consideration to this Model Law while enacting or revising their respective Laws.
 The IT Bill, 1999 is a sequel to this U.N. resolution. Malaysia has introduced new comprehensive legislation whereas
 countries like USA, European Union, Singapore, Korea, Japan, UK and Germany have brought out multiple
 amendments to the in existing laws as well as enacted new legislation. Italy, Japan, South Korea, Sweden and UK have
 also introduced Digital Signature laws recently.
9. In India, an Inter-Ministerial Standing Committee under the Chairmanship of the Secretary to the then Department of
 Electronics was set up on 15
th September, 1997 to take stock of draft legislation and formulate a draft Bill on electronic
 data transfer and transactions having regard to international practices. The interim report of the Standing Committee
 recommended amendments in the existing core laws such as the Indian Evidence Act, 1872; the General Clauses Act.,
 1897 and the Indian Penal Code and that there should be a single comprehensive cyber law covering digital signature,
 data protection and computer offences. Hence, the Information Technology(IT) Bill.
10. The IT Bill provides a peripheral framework for e-commerce regime, which comprises of 93 sections divided into
 13 chapters. It includes four schedules which lay down the relative amendments sought to be made to the Indian Penal
 Code, the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the Banker’s Evidence Act, 1891, and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The
 13 chapters respectively deal with preliminary matters, digital signature, electronic governance, attribution,
 acknowledgement and dispatch of electronic records, secure electronic records and secure digital signatures, regulation
 of certifying authorities, digital signature certificates, obligations of subscribers, penalties and adjudication, the cyber
 regulations appellate tribunal, offences, network service providers not to be liable in certain cases and miscellaneous
 provisions.
11. The Committee observes that the Bill provides: -
i. to facilitate electronic communication by means of reliable electronic records;
ii. to facilitate electronic inter-action in trade and commerce, eliminate barriers to electronic commerce resulting
 from uncertainties over writing and signature
requirements, and to promote the development of the legal and business
infrastructure necessary to implement secure electronic commerce;

79th Report on the Information Technology Bill, 1999
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/79report.htm[29-08-2018 16:16:19]
iii. to facilitate electronic filing of documents with government agencies and statutory corporations, and to promote
 efficient delivery of government services by means of reliable electronic records;
iv. to minimise the incidence of forged electronic records, intentional and unintentional alteration of records, and
 fraud, forgery or falsification in electronic commerce and other electronic transactions;
v. to help establish uniformity of rules, regulations and standards regarding the authentication and integrity of
 electronic records or documents; and
vi. to promote public confidence in the integrity and reliability of electronic records and electronic commerce, and to
 foster ‘the development of electronic commerce through the use of electronic signatures to lend authenticity and
 integrity to correspondence in any electronic medium.
vii. To provide for a Cyber Regulations Advisory Committee consisting of a Chairperson and such other number of
 official and non-official members as may be prescribed by rules to be made by the Central Government.
viii. to provide for penalties for contravention of the regulations made under the Act.
ix. To provide for the establishment of Cyber Regulations appellate Tribunal with the same composition and powers
 as that of the appellate Tribunal constituted under the Securities Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 and to hear

x. to provide for the deposit of the penalty amount as a prerequisite for filing of appeal before the Appellate

12. The Committee considered the Information Technology Bill, 1999 in its meetings held on 25
th & 27th April, 2nd, 3rd
 , 4th and 8th May, 2000.
13. The Secretary and the Representatives of the Ministry of Information Technology apprised the Committee about the
 need to provide legal recognition to transactions carried out by
means of electronic data interchange and other means of electronic communication and the developments leading to the
 drafting of the Bill.
14. In the meetings of the Committee, Chairman, Telecom Commission made a presentation on the subject matter of the
 Bill and expressed their concern on the issue of "Convergence" of the Telecommunication, Broadcasting and
 Information Technology, as intended to be covered under the Bill. According to him, the convergence of technologies
 will result in the dilution of the boundaries between different sectors and it may be difficult to distinguish the computer
 networks’ as defined in the Bill from the telecom network. Therefore, the issues and concerns relating to security and
 privacy of information in the Bill would be more or less similar to the concerns in the area of telecommunications and
 distribution of encrypted TV or Radio programmes. The Secretary, Ministry of Information & Broadcasting also
 echoed the same apprehension. The Chairman, Telecom Commission also suggested for inclusion of word "voice" in
 the definition of "information" as given in clause 2(u) of the Bill to avoid any overlapping with the provisions of the
 Indian Telegraph Act; and to fix a time limit for retention of electronic records in clause 7 of the Bill. In response to the
 latter, Member Secretary, Law Commission of India submitted that the provision of Public Records Act will mutatis
 mutandis apply to this Act. Moreover, the electronic records automatically start vanishing after 5-6 years.
15. The Representatives of the Indian Music Industry and the National Association of Software and Service Companies
 (NASSCOM) also appeared before the Committee on the subject matter of the Bill. Both the representatives expressed
 the need for deletion of clause 78 of the Bill as the same appears to be in conflict with the provisions of the Copyright
 Act. Moreover, in view of the defence of due diligence and knowledge being available under clause 78, representatives
 were of the view that it was difficult to book the violators as clause 78 merely required a Network Service Provider
 with knowledge of an offence to prove that it exercised due diligence to prevent the commission of the offence. The
 Indian Music Industry submitted that the tests of lack of knowledge or of due diligence as stipulated in clause 78 of the
 IT Bill were not precise and objective and a Network Service Provider (NSP) or intermediary could rely upon clause 78

 the concept of cyber law is of recent origin.
16. The Committee in its meeting held on 4
th May, 2000 had the benefit of the presentation made by the Commissioner
 of Police(CP), Delhi. The CP stated, inter alia, that in order to prevent cyber crimes, all Internet Service Providers
 should allow internet access through the digital telephone only which would enable to keep records of caller
 identification in the respective server. He also expressed concern on the mushrooming of Cyber Cafes from where a
 criminal mind could easily cause damage in economic terms. In order to provide solution, he suggested insertion of a
 provision regarding identification of particulars of the user through ration card, electoral card, passport, driving license,
 PAN Card etc. An obligation should be imposed on the ISP to maintain a record the users and provide details of every
 cyber activity. The Commissioner of Police informed the Committee that though at present not much police force is
 equipped with cyber knowledge yet initiatives have already been made and various training courses were going on to
 educate the police officials. The Commissioner, of Police, however disagreed with clause 77 which deputes an officer
 of the rank of Deputy Superintendent Police or above to investigate the offences under the Bill. According to him what
 was required is the knowledge of computer, not the rank and even an Inspector or Sub-Inspector could be competent to
 investigate the offences if he possessed the knowledge of the computer. The Commissioner of Police submitted that the
 officers of the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police were already over burdened and by assigning the job of
 investigation to them, little time would be left for him to attend to other work. After hearing the Commissioner of
 Police, the Committee suggested for recruitment of persons possessing the knowledge and experience in computer and
 also create special task force to tackle cyber crimes.

Introduction
 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the
 Committee to submit the report on its behalf, present the Eighth Report on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the
 Department of Biotechnology (Ministry of Science and Technology) for the year 1994-95 (Demand No. 73).
2. The Committee held three meetings on March 23, 24 and April 7, 1994 (Annexure). In the meeting held on March 23,
 while considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Biotechnology, the Committee sought detailed
 clarifications on various development projects, programmes and schemes which fall within the mandate of the
 Department. On its sitting held on March 24, the representatives of the Department replied to the clarifications sought
 by the Hon'ble Members. The Committee wishes to express 'its thanks to the officers of the Department of
 Biotechnology for placing before it the required material and answering the queries-raised by the Hon'ble Members on
 various aspects of the Projects and Programmes administered by the Department to enable it to thoroughly scrutinise,
 the Demands for Grants of the Department of Biotechnology.
3. The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on April 7, 1994

April 7, 1994
SYED SIBTEY RAZ

REPORT
Biotechnology is an inter-disciplinary field in which rapid advances are taking place the world over. Applications of
 biotechnology can lead to the development of processes which can contribute significantly to agricultural production
 and industrial growth. In the medical field too biotechnology has many important and growing beneficial applications.
 There are many other sectors of economy which can benefit tremendously by the application of biotechnology. This

2. The Secretary of the Department of Bio-technology informed the Committee that the Department of Biotechnology
 has made steady progress· during the year 1993~94 in fulfilling its mandate. He particularly referred to basic research,
 product based R&D projects, demonstrations and transfer of technologies, manufacturing activities; manpower
 development and generation of new products and processes. He informed the Committee about the new initiatives taken
 up last year which would lead to sharply focused research based products and activities. The Committee was also
 informed about the proposed programmes of the Department for the year 1994-95 which were mainly concerned with
 research and development, experimental field demonstrations, manpower development, creation of. infrastructure
 facilities, activities of the autonomous institutions and public undertakings of the Department, international
 collaboration, bio-safety and programmes for the weaker sections.            
3. After listening to' the presentation made by the Secretary of the Department of Biotechnology, the Committee
 examined the budgetary allocations made for various programmes falling within the mandate of the Department.
 *
While examining the Demands for Grants of the Department of Biotechnology, the Committee also got an opportunity
 to assess the progress of various ongoing programmes of the Department.
4. The budget estimates for the Department of Biotechnology for the year 1994-95 are places at Rs. 90.23 crores, 'of
 which 87.00 crores form the plan component and Rs. 3.23 crores form the non-plan component. The Committee is
 pleased that such a large part of the budget is under Plan, reflecting new initiatives that are monitored for useful and
 results, and not under non-plan which normally reflects only the running of an existing set-up. The budget estimates for
 the Department for the year 1993-94 were Rs. 88.10 crores, out of which the plan component was Rs. 85.00 crores and
 non-plan was Rs. 3.10 crores. Comparing the budgetary outlay of the Department. for the year 199~-95 with the outlay
 earmarked for the year 1993-94, 1992-93 and 1991 .. 92 the Committee found that the position with regard to the
 utilisation of the plan component of the annual allocation by the Department has greatly' improved. In the year 1991-92
 the approved plan outlay was Rs. 71.00 crores, while the utilisation was Rs. 61.34 crores. In the year 1992-93, the
 approved plan outlay was Rs. 80.33 crores and the Department could utilise Rs. 73.16 crores. In the year 1993-94 the
 situation further improved with regard to the plan component of .the budgetary allocation. Out of the approved outlay
 of Rs. 85.00 crores, the Department could utilise a sum of Rs. 84.95 crores. The Committee expresses its satisfaction
 over the narrowing down of the gap between the approved plan outlay and its utilisation and hopes that this- trend
 would be maintained during the current financial year as well.
5. The Committee wanted to know as to how much of the total allocation agreed to by the planning Commission during
 the Eighth plan period has been received by the Department year­wise under different heads, and what is the balance
 amount left. The Committee was told that the Department of Biotechnology projected an outlay of Rs. 650.00 crores for
 the entire Eighth Plan period. The Planning Commission had tentatively agreed to an outlay of Rs. 450.00 crores, but
 the indicative outlay for the Department has been kept at Rs. 265.00 crores. The scheme-wise allocation as demanded

The Committee expresses its anxiety that during the Eighth Plan period (1992-97) the annual plan allocations made to
 the Department, while exceeding the indicative plan outlay, will still fall short of the total Plan outlay of Rs. 450.00
 crores, unless there is a major step up in the last two years of the Plan. In view of the laudable objectives being pursued
 by the Department and the progress made by the Department in the use of biotechnology in the area of agriculture,
 industrial development and prevention and control of diseases, the Committee would like to reiterate its earlier
 recommendation made in the Fifth Report that the allocation of Rs. 450.00 crores tentatively agreed by the Planning
 Commission should actually be given to the Department so that the current programmes of the Department and the
 projects undertaken by it do not get adversely affected due to lack of sufficient funds. The Committee hopes that the
 Planning Commission while· doing mid-term appraisal of the Eighth Five Year Plan would enhance the allocation of
 the Department.
The Committee observed that under the head 'Basic and Product Based R&D Projects allocation has been made for the

7. On being asked why no provision has been made for the Oil Palm Demonstration Project in the budget estimates for
 the year 1994-95, the Committee was told that the Project taken up in the state of Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and
 Karnataka has been completed. The Department did not propose to expand the project further, though several R&D
 projects on oil palm like tissue culture, pollination, oil quality, etc. would be taken up and these will be covered under
 the 'Basic and Product based R&D Projects'. The Committee is happy to note that the Oil Palm Demonstration Project
 has been completed but would like the Department to devote its efforts towards R&D pertaining to oil palm and give
 more attention to the developing of a package on feasibility and performance of oil palm under different climatic
 'conditions as this would help more farmers in the country.
8. The Committee is aware of the fact that biofertilisers cannot totally replace chemical fertilisers. Biofertilisers, by
 adding organic matter, help in maintaining the soil health. Their use can contribute to reduced requirement of chemical
 fertilisers in intensive agriculture. They can be of relevance to special crops and agroecological situations:'" As per the
 information furnished by the Department in the area of Demonstration with regard to Blue Green Algae (BGA) during
 the year 1993-94 there were 1500 demoristrations conducted and about 600 production ponds were made. 38 tonnes of
 BGA was produced and the increase in the paddy yield ranged from about 5 to 14 percent. As regards Rhizobium, 224
 field trials were done and three training programme were organised. In the area· of biological control of crop pests, the
 crops covered were sugarcane, cotton, chickpea, tobacco, tomato, groundnut, sunflowers, blackgram, green- gram,
 pigeonpea, sesamum, cauliflower and brinjal. Two production units were also set up. In view of the importance of
 biofertilisers and biopesticides which are. eco-friendly and safer, the Committee expresses its satisfaction over the' fact
 that the Department is having two separate Mission Mode Projects, one on Technology development and demonstration
 of biofertilisers and the other on the development, production and demonstration of biological pest control agents.
9. The Committee noticed that investment in the' Indian Vaccine Corporation Limited was made to the tune of Rs.
 148.00 lakhs, as per the revised estimates for the year 1993-94 but in the budget estimates for the year 1994-95, the
 allocation has come down to Rs. 10.00 lakhs only. The Department explained that this joint sector project with French
 collaboration is under re-negotiation to finalise the 'product mix'. Depending on the outcome of the negotiations with
 the French Company, the project would be re-defined and investment decision would be taken. Due to this a token
 provision of Rs. IO.OO lakhs has been made. The Committee, therefore, recommends that concerted efforts should be
 made to finalise the negotiations with a view to implementing the project. The Committee agrees that the use of Oral
 Polio Vaccine is very vital for control of polio in India and the Department should make every effort to ensure adequate
 reliable supplies of this vaccine to control and largely eliminate polio from India.
10. The Committee wanted to know the reasons as to why a provision of Rs. 64.50 lakhs has been made in the budget
 estimates for the year 1994-95 under Allowance (other than travel expenses) while in the revised estimates for 1993-94
 the sum under this category was Rs. 48.00 lakhs only? The Committee was informed that this increase is partly due to
 the expectation that the vacant posts in the Department would be filled up during the year 1994-95. At present there are
 52 posts lying vacant in the Department. The Committee is firmaly of the view that due to inadequate staffing the
 programmes undertaken by the Department may get adeversely affected and in this regard the Committee had in its
 Fifth Report already recommended for the filling up of the vacant positions in the Department. The Committee hopes
 that during the year 1994-95 most of the vacancies existing in the Department would be filled up. The Committee is
 firmly of the view that no time should be wasted on bureaucratic aspects in this regard. The Department was created out
 of the Department of Science and Technology and is part of the Ministry of Science & Technology, personal policies,
 recruitment rules, etc, already exist in the Department of Science & Technology and can be made use of without delay;

 the Department has also exemption from UPSC which should continue. The Committee is of the view that so far
 nothing significant has been done to attract Indian scientists working abroad into our country. For encouraging our
 scientists working in other countries to return to India what is important is that scientists working in the country should
 be well paid and special efforts are made to provide them proper accommodation and other facilities. They should be
 allowed to work in a free atmosphere; rather than in a system which is too much rule-ridden.
11. The Committee pointed out that in the budgetary outlay for 1994-95 for creating infrast­ructural facilities the
 Department had demanded Rs. 10.00 crores, while it was given a sum of Rs. 7.90 crores. In view of this gap the
 Committee specifically wanted to know as to how the Department would be able to work in the area of creating infra
 structural facilities for its various programmes. The representative of the Department informed the Committee that the
 Planning Commission is of the view that the Department has already created several infrastructural facilities for
 collection, maintenace and supply of biotechnological material. Funds are also provided to the host institutions for
 undertaking various R&D programmes. Planning Commission is, therefore, of the view that efforts should be made to
 transfer some of these facilities to host institutions for maintenance of the facilities and Department of Biotechnology
 may provide research support on project-mode basis, and that it would not be appropriate to support such facilities for
 an indefinite period. The Committee was also informed that the Department of Biotechnology and Department of
 Science and Technology along with the CSIR and other Ministries are now making efforts to provide joint funding for a
 number of facilities. While the Committee agrees that joint funding of high-tech facilities involving large sum of money
 may be implemented, what is important is to ensure that such facilities are shared and fully utilized by the user
 Departments and all those in the country who need them and can benefit from them. The Committee is of the view that
 the facilities so set up should be made use of to the fullest extent; and it is the institutional set up for this to which
 attention needs to be devoted; since funding, whether through one Department or on a multi-institutional basis, is all by
 Government.
12. The Committee evinced keen interest in the immunological approaches to fertility. control and wanted to know
 whether any time-schedule has been fixed to arrive at some definite approaches. The Committee was informed that the
 project on immunological approaches to fertility control was launched in 1987 and has gone behind schedule, After
 completion of phase-II clinical trials, a decision was taken that there should be an extended phase-II clinical trials by
 the Expert Committee. With the approval of the Drugs Controller of India the Department has taken on these extended
 phase-II clinical trials. At the end of 1995, when the extended phase-II clinical trial enters the phase-III clinical trial, the
 Department would be able to give a time-schedule about the availability of vaccine in the market. The representative of
 the Department informed that the development of vaccine generally takes 10 to 15 years. The Committee shares the
 concern of the Department of Biotechnology in ensuring that the product which would ultimately result from the
 researches conducted by the Department should be totally 'safe and acceptable.
13. Under the project on semi-intensive prawn aquaculture a production of 10tlhalyr in two crops was demonstrated and
 the average production in the final crop was 5.49tA1a and production levels went as high as 6.7t1ha. The programme
1
 according to the Department, has given a great impetus to prawn farming by demonstrating techno-economic viability
 of the system. The Department is having a Missiun Mode Project on semi-intensive prawn aquaculture for freshwater,
 brackishwater and marine species. The Committee was also given to understand that the feed developed at the Central
 Food Technological Research Institute (CFTRI), Mysore, tested in a Semi-intensive prawn aquaculture system, gave
 results comparable to imported feeds. The cost of the feed comes to Rs. 25.00 per kg. as against about Rs. 35.00 per kg.
 of the imported feed. The indigenous feed developed at CFTRI, Mysore has been tried at Nellore in the semi­-
intensive aquaculture where the production level was 5t1ha/crop as against that of imported feed in which the average
 production level is 5.49t/ha/crop. The indigenous feed developed is still to be transferred to the industry for large scale
 production. The Committee observes that India has a vast coast line. There is, therefore, a great possibility to increasing
 prawn yields. lnstead of restricting to a few varieties, possibilities should be explored to develop many other varieties
 and this is an area which needs to be strengthened. The Department should make efforts to transfer the technology of
 producing feed to companies and ensure joint B&D industry work on this which would enable the country to save on
 the importing of feed. The Department should also devote itself to the developing of seed. To meet the shortage of
 prawn seed more hatcheries should be set up for developing seed and in this regard greater coordination is required
 among the Department of Biotechnology; the Ministry of Agriculture and the concerned Departments of the State
 Governments.
14. The Committee expressed its serious concern over the rapidly increasing number of AIDS victims in the country and
 wanted to know whether the Department has developed some indigenous tests which are less costly than the imported
 test kits. The Committee was informed that the kits currently used by the National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO)

 order .to develop indigenous capability for detecting HIV infection, Debarment of Biotechnology has taken up R&D

 the National Institute of Immunology, New Delhi and the third, on the WB method (for HIV-I only) at the Cancer
 Research Institute, Bombay had been sanctioned in September, 1993. The progress so far has been very good and it is
 anticipated that the testing format would be ready towards the end of 1995. The Committee is of the view that this area
 needs special attention of the Department and hopes that the Department would be able to develop indigenous kits for
 the detection of AIDS which would result in saving foreign exchange and easy availability of the kits.
15. The Committee was told that more bio-technology based projects would be generated for the uplift of the SC/ST
 population and other weaker sections in different parts of the country. There is already an expert committee appointed
 to develop biotechnology based programmes for these sections of society,. The Committee has noted with satisfaction
 that in the budget estimates for the year 1994-95 the allocation made for the biotechnology programmes for the
 Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes has increased from Rs. 50.00 lakhs made last year .to Rs. 100.00 lakhs this year
 and recommends that the new technologies developed by the Department should lay special emphasis on the needs of
 the women. The new technologies should aim at making them economically self-sufficient which would naturally
 enhance their social status. This programme also requires greater coordination among the socio-economic Ministries
 and con­cerned departments of the State Governments.
16. The Committee also wanted to know about the monitoring mechanism which the Department has evolved over the
 years to evaluate the efficiency and output of the projects administered by it; and the exact criteria which the
 Department adopts while assessing the efficiency of its programmes and the results achieved by it. The Committee was
 informed that the Department has been working with the expert advice of 13 Task Forces. 4 new Task Forces have been
 set up recently. These Task Forces help in monitoring the project through evaluation, written progress reports,
 presentations, site visits, and in-depth discussions with Project Inves­tigators. The monitoring mechanism is being
 further strengthened with more frequent site visits through Expert Committees in which generally a member 'of the
 Task Force is associated. An annual review is a regular feature. The criteria used for judging the performance of a
 project are as follows :
 
Progress vis-a-vis each objective
 Number of publications
(c) Ph.D. Thesis
(d) No. of trained  manpower
 (e) Patents
(f) New products or processes
(g) Technology package
(h) Societal impact
17. The Committee notes that this Department is the nodal department for biotechnology and the results stemming from
 its work have to be implemented through other Ministries of the Government of India and of the State Governments
 concerned with food, health, industry, etc. The latter have to ensure large scale field demonstrations, availability of
 inputs and final effective utilization. It is, therefore, essential to have appropriate high level institutional set up for
 coordination and effective project management. This issue and the related aspect of setting up a Biotechnology
 Commission will be considered by the Committee when it further examines the work of this Department. Meanwhile,
 the Department should give thought to these questions.
18. After making a detailed scrutiny of the Demands for Grants of the Department of Bio-technology and assessing the
 progress of various important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the
 Demands for Grants of Rs. 90.23 crores, as sought by the Department of Biotechnology for the year 1994-95, under
 demand No. 73", are in order and may be approved.

Action taken by the Department 
      The observation of  the Committee that  ‘there are certain unexp lored areas in the fiel

with the emphasis given b y the NII, and th e Institute has been continuousl y focussin g its rese
activities in unexplored areas including Immunodiagnostics, diseases, as well as their basis. 
      As a result, NII has developed immunodia gnostic tests for a number  of diseases such as v
hepatitis, t yphoid fever, amoebic liver abscess and strep tococcal infection, as well as for pre gna
detection.  All these technologies have  been licensed  to  the  pharmaceutical  industry  
 for commercialization.  Commercialization has not yet been completed in those cases where the In

      However, NII continues its efforts.  Du ring the year 2000-2001, NII has focused on a simple tes
detecting tuberculosis, whic h will soon be read y for transfer to industrial partners for eve n

      In the area of diseases unexplored as yet, NII has initiated research on number of such cases.

      Regarding raising funds, NII has some pharmaceutical fundin g for basic research.  Hoechst I

provide close intellectual and infras tructural support to the biotechnolo gy industry through the j

INTRODUCTION 
  
            I, the Chairman of the Departme nt-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology,
Environment & Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this
Eighty-fourth Report on the Action Taken by the Department  of Space on the recommendations contained in the
Seventy-seventh Report of the Committee on Demands for Grants (2000-2001) of the Department of Space. 
  
2.         The Report of the Committee deals with  the Action Taken by the Department of Space on the
recommendations contained in the Se venty-seventh Report of the Depart ment-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Fo rests on the Demands for Grants (2000-2001) of the 
Department of Space which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 24th April, 2000. 
  
3.         There are eleven recommendations containe d in the Seventy-seventh Repo rt of the Committee.  Action 
Taken Notes on the recommend ations of the Committee, were received from the De partment on 4th December,
2000. 
  
4.         In the meeting held on 27 th March, 2001, the Committee consider ed the draft Action Taken Report and 
adopted the same. 
  
  
 
NEW DELHI                                                                                                                     C. RAMACHANDRAIAH,
March 27, 2001                                                                                                                     Chairman, 
                      Committee on Science & Technology, 
                         Environment & Forests.     
 
R E  P O R  T 
  
The Report of the Committee deals with the Acti on Taken by the Department of Space on the
recommendations contained in the Se venty-seventh Report of the Depart ment-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Fo rests on the Demands for Grants (2000-2001) of the 
Department of Space which was presented to the Ra jya Sabha on 24th April, 2000.  There are eleven
recommendations contained in the Seventy-seventh Re port of the Committee. Action Taken notes on the
recommendations of the Committee was received from the Department on 4th  December, 2000. 
On scrutiny of the Action Taken Note s as received from the Department of Space, the Committee finds tha t
all the eleven recommendations have been fully implemented.   
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken 
by the Department of Space are given in the succeeding paragraphs: - 
Launch Vehicles 
Recommendation 
      The Committee observes India is on e of the six countries with homemade satellites in orbit. Despite 
being a new entrant to the competitive global space club, India’s overall track record both in the field o f 
rocketry and satellites has been impressive. This , of co urse, does not overlook the fact that it had its share
of failures too, which needless to say can be expected in any hi-tech project. To cite a few, one can recall the 
failure of the ASLV and PSLV. But these failed missions onl
y proved to be another ste p on the ladder to
Page 3 of 9R E P O R T
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/84th.htm

success. The subsequent flights we re a resounding success. This endorse d India’s claim to be a growing 
super power. The Committee, however, would like th e Department to keep the analysis of each failed
mission in view so that corrective measures can be taken while executing future programmes. 
(Para 6)
Action taken by the Department 
      The observation of the Committee is noted. 
Comments 
      The Committee notes the reply and hopes that self- appraisal of the projects w ill enable the Department o f
Space to counter any possible failures.       
Satellite Navigation   
Recommendation 
      The Committee feels that in order to fall in  the line with international standards, the Department
should consider establishing a satellite based naviga tion system as that would facilitate modern air
navigation system.  The Committee is of the view th at the Airport Authority of India and the Department
of Space should work in close co-ordination to achieve the objective.  
(Para 13.2)
Action taken by the Department 
      The Department of Space is working in close co-o peration with Airports Authority of India in defining  a 
modern  satellite  based  air  navigation  system.  This   system  will  be  in  line   with  
  
International standards.  As a first step a Tech nology Demonstration System (TDS) for Space Based
Augmentation System (SBAS) has been worked out jointly with Airports Authority of India for implementation. 
Comments 
      While the Committee commends the efforts made by the Department for opera tionalising the TDS, it would,
however, like to be apprised of the pr ogress made in this dir ection at the time of consid eration of next year’s 
budgetary grants. 
Indian Remote Sensing Satellite 
Recommendation 
While the Committee appreciates the efforts being ma de by the Department in  augmenting its remote
sensing capability, what is important is not only e ffective management and utilization of natural resources
but locating more of such resources considering that such resources are on the verge of depletion in the
times ahead.  The Committee therefore observes that th e efforts should be so oriented with emphasis on
mapping more of natural resources as also the optimum utilization of the resources already tapped.  
(Para 14.2)
Action taken by the Department 
      As a nodal agency for the National Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS), Department of Space
has been interacting with the user agencies through various Standing Committees under NNRMS to co-ordinate 
various user projects.  Through the unique NNRMS arra ngements, the country has es tablished a comprehensive
institutional framework, technological capability and applications  expertise involving cent ral, state governments
and private entrepreneurs.  The responsibility of DOS is limited to helping the users in generating appropriate
information using satellite remote se nsing and collateral data for optimum  exploitation of natural resources. 
Ultimately, it is the user department s, which have to make use of the information made av ailable from remote
sensing for ground level implementation.  It is the end eavor of DOS to lay emphasis on mapping of natural
resources and assist in sustainable utilisation of the resources.  For example, in the area of ground water resources,
which are fast depleting, the Ministry of Rural Deve lopment under the National Dr inking Water Mission, has
Page 4 of 9R E P O R T
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/84th.htm

launched a major project in close co -ordination with National Remote Sens ing Agency to identify drinking wate r
sources in 1.1 lakh habitations in the first phase.  The pr oject also envisages ground water recharging, an essential
element in conserving the depleting wa ter resources.  NRSA is preparing detailed hydro-geomorphological maps 
giving full details for ground level implementation by Minist ry of Rural Development.  Similar projects are taken
up by various State Remote Sensing Centers also at the behest of the user agencies.  In addition, many States have
launched State Natural Resources Ma nagement System (SNRMS ) to actively coordinate the activities amongs t
various user departments to ensure  integration of remote sensing- based information with conventional data.  I t 
can, thus, be said, efforts are on at both Central and St ate level to effectively utilize the remote sensing based
information for sustainable utilization of natural resources. 
Comments 
      The Committee appreciates the work done by Depart ment of Space in mapping natural resources.  However,
being nodal agency of National Natural Resources Management System, the  
  
Department of Space should play a leading role in bringing better coordination with user agencies so as to achieve
optimum results from the programme. 
Integrated Mission for Sustainable Development(IMSD) 
Recommendation 
      The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation (68 th Report) that even though the programme 
was heading towards a right direction, the pace of the programme appeared slow.  The Committee feels
that the tempo of the programme needs to be geared up and it should have time bound targets.  
(Para 15.4)
Action taken by the Department 
The major aim of IMSD is to prepare scientific actio n plans for sustainable development of land and wate r
resources on watershed basis using satellite remote sensin g  data and other conventi onal collateral data. Unde r
IMSD, preparation of action plans was taken up in 24 7 study areas (i.e. 97% of the study area) have been
completed, the remaining study areas being in J&K,  Nagaland and Megha laya, wherein the work could no t
progress due to ground realities.  The outputs in terms of maps, accompanied with reports, which could be utilized
for preparing development plans by the district admini stration have been handed over to the district/State
administration.  While the DOS has th e programmatic responsibility for co ordinating the preparation of action
plan maps, the responsibility for the ground implemen tation of the action plans rest with the State
departments/district administration.  The centrally sponsored schemes such as NWDPRA/DDP would also help
the States to implement the action plan s.  DOS has taken proactive role to  catalyze ground implementation of the
action plans and towards this, DOS has been pursuing with Ministry of Rural Development for modification and
revision of watershed development gu idelines to appropriately incorporat e and institutionalize the use of IMSD
action plan in their implementation. 
Comments 
      The Committee notes the position.
 
Disaster Management System  
Recommendation 
      The Committee is constrained to observe that the perfection in the functioning of the Cyclone Warning
Dissemination Systems (CWDS) for predicting the cont ours of the cyclone is yet to be achieved. The
country has witnessed the fury of weather Gods in the form of cyclones and  other weather extremes
resulting in tremendous loss of life and property  in some States.  There is thus an imperative need to
perfect the system.  The projects therefore need to be taken up with sense of urgenc y and, if necessary, in  
co-operation with other Department s and agencies.  The Committee feel s that the constraint of funds 
should not be allowed to stand in the totality of these projects. 
(Para 16.4)       
Page 5 of 9R E P O R T
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/84th.htm

Action taken by the Department 
      Weather forecasting including  predicting the cyclones in the coun try is done by India Meteorological 
Department.  There  has  been  continuous   effort  in  the country to improve and  
perfect the weather forecast services by improvin g the data modeling and the related computer and
communication infrastructure.  The CWDS is a part of the cyclone prediction and warning system and efforts are
on to modernise  the CWDS with digital version. 
Comments 
      While the Committee notes the reply, it observ es that some time-frame s hould be fixed for complete 
modernization of  the CWDS, so as to pre-empt the frequent attacks  of any catastrophe in one or other part of the
country.        
Cryo-Upper Stage (CUS) Project 
Recommendation 
      The Committee observes that there is imperative need for the country to perfect its cryogenic 
capabilities.  Sustained effort and perseverance should he lp in that direction.  Added to this the analysis o f
past experiments would act as a guidance to the future. 
      (Para 18.4)
Action taken by the Department 
The observation of the Committee is noted. 
Comments 
      The Committee notes the reply.        
Direct-to-Home (DTH) TV Mission 
Recommendation 
The Committee feels that the Government should clear the fog on the issue as early as possible
or else its credibilit y to spread information technolo gy is bound to suffer. DTH is a part o f
information technolo gy and Government should cl ear the hurdles on the sub ject keepin g the
interest of the viewers uppermost while enacting any law on the subject. 
 (Para  19.1)
Action taken by the Department 
DTH policy has been cleared by the Union Cabinet in November, 2000 allowing Indian Companies to set up
DTH broadcast services.  Ministry of Information and Broadcasting will evolve guid elines/procedures in this
regard and issue necessary licenses for this service 
Comments 
      The Committee notes the reply. 
Second Launch Pad Project 
Recommendation         
The Committee feels that as the number of  launche s per year increases the need to have a second
launch pad cannot be underestimated.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the development o f
second launch pad should be accorded priority keeping in view of the requirements in this regard. 
             (Para 20.3)  
  
  
Page 6 of 9R E P O R T
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/science/84th.htm

Action Taken by the Department 
The observation of the Committee is noted. 
Comments 
      The Committee notes the position.
 
Development Educational & Communication Unit 
Recommendation 
      The Committee observes that  the Department is pro gressing w e l l  i n  i t s  p l a n  t o  e x t e n d  t h e
TDCC/JDCP pro jects to other states as well. The Comm ittee, however, observes that before
opening new fronts, the Department should  evaluate the results of the projects already in hand.  
                                                                                                                              (Para 23.3) 
Action Taken by the Department 
      The Department has already taken action for evalua tion of the Jhabua Develo pment Communication Projec t
(JDCP). 
Comments       
      The Committee commends the Department for show ing keen interest in the programme.  However, i t
recommends that more emphasis is required to be  given for wider dissemination of knowledge about the
programme. 
Sponsored Research Programme (RESPOND) 
Recommendation 
The Committee recommends that apart from initiating the research projects in the academic intuitions,
the Department should constantly monitor the perfor mance of these projects so that country could be
benefited by the completion of these projects.  It should be the endeavor of the Department to complete the
projects within the stipulated time frame.               
(Para 24.2)
Action taken by the Department 
The Department has instituted a system to review pe riodically the progress of the projects sponsored unde
r
RESPOND.  Committees have be en constituted at each ISRO Centre for this purpose.  The above review process
also identifies action wherever necessary to ensure the completion of the Project within the stipulated time frame. 
Comments 
The Committee notes the reply. 
Antrix Corporation 
Recommendation 
The Committee is happ y to note that Antrix Corporation is pro gressing well in
commercialising Indian Space product and services in the hi ghly competitive international space
market and that will set a stage  for further boost to the In dia’s multi faceted space pro gramme.  
E f f o r t  s h o u l d  b e  m a d e  t o  s e c u r e  the wider involvement  of the Industr y in marketin g and other
areas of its activities 
(Para 26.3)
Action taken by the Department 
Antrix has been putting  in concerte d efforts to maximally utilize the indu strial capability and support.  The
areas where Antrix continues to work closely with industries are for the ha rdware for launch services, hardware
and software required for the up gradation of international ground st ations receiving IRS data, supply o f
Page 7 of 9R E P O R T

spacecraft components and subsystems for international space agencies etc. 
The agreement with Space Imaging of USA for the acce ss and global marketing of remote sensing data has
now fructified with more than ten st ations across the globe now accessing and receiving IRS data.  The hardware
for the stations continue to be supplied by Indian Industrie s.  Discussions are being he ld with other international
space companies for the dissemination of  IRS data.  Efforts are on to bring in private agencies for the marketing
of remote sensing data in India, thus paving the way for private service providers in  this area. 
In the Satcom area, the announceme nt of the Satcom Policy has thrown  open a number of opportunities fo r
industry participation.  Antrix is currently exploring the market for te lecommunication satellite for private secto r
service providers. 
Launch services (for launching satellites) are expected to form a significant part of Antrix activities.  An
understanding has been reac hed with Arianspace to enlarge the launc h opportunities for small satellites using
complementary capabilities.  This is expected to provide increased scope for industrial participation. 
Comments 
      The Committee notes with satisfactio n the efforts made by the Corporat ion in augmenting the marketing o f 
Indian space products and would like th e Corporation to vigorously pursue its efforts to consolidate its position in
the space market.

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment &
 Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Eighty-fifth Report on the Action
 Taken by the Department of Ocean Development on the recommendations contained in the Seventy-sixth Report of the Committee on
 Demands for Grants (2000-2001) of the Department of Ocean Development.
 
            The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Ocean Development  on the recommendations
 contained in the Seventy-sixth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology,
 Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2000-2001) of the Department of Ocean Development  which was presented to
 the Rajya Sabha on 24th April, 2000.
 
            There are fourteen recommendations contained in the Seventy-sixth Report of the Committee.  Action Taken Notes on the
 recommendations of the Committee, were received from the Department on 20th  December, 2000.

April 9, 2001                                                                                                                             Chairman,
